standard.title: Drama across cultures and contexts
standard.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience drama
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify arts works in their lives and explain a simple reason why the arts are important for people and communities (Foundation). They have not yet explored drama specifically across different cultures and contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and other contexts experience drama.

nodes.label: Where drama happens in life and community
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify places and occasions where drama is experienced — at school, in the community, and beyond.
nodes.minimum_width: Student identifies at least one context where drama is experienced beyond their classroom (a school performance, a community event, a screen-based drama).
nodes.typical_width: Students share experiences of attending drama performances or participating in drama at school and in their community; they discuss where and why drama is made and experienced.
wider: Students explore drama contexts from another culture or region (e.g. shadow puppetry, Asian performance traditions, community storytelling theatre) and compare with familiar drama
Students consider how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own communities through stories, traditions and shared experience
nodes.hinge_reason: If students only understand drama as a school classroom activity, they cannot engage with the 'across cultures and contexts' scope of the descriptor; understanding that drama exists widely is the foundation for the 'why' inquiry.

response_modes.reason: Deliberately expand students' awareness of drama contexts — community theatre, cultural ceremonies, puppetry, screen drama — before narrowing to 'why' questions.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of drama contexts — community, cultural, cross-cultural, historical — that students can explore is very broad; wider engagement here builds a much richer frame for understanding drama's social and cultural purposes.
success_criteria: Student names at least two different contexts where drama is experienced (e.g. at school, at a community event, on screen)
Student asks or responds to at least one question about where or why drama is made

nodes.label: How and why drama communicates — across cultures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how drama communicates feelings and ideas, and identify that different communities and cultures use drama for different purposes.
nodes.minimum_width: Student can explain one reason why people in a specific context make and experience drama.
nodes.typical_width: Students recognise how drama shows feelings and ideas people have about the world; they ask and discuss questions ('How and why are these people making drama?', 'What is the drama about?'); they explore how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own and other communities.
wider: Students investigate how drama communicates stories from a country or region in Asia, exploring what that drama is about and why it matters to that community
Students compare two different drama contexts — one familiar and one from another culture — and identify similarities and differences in purpose and form

response_modes.reason: Use guiding questions ('What is the drama about?', 'How do you think the people making it feel?', 'Why would a community share this story?') to scaffold simple causal and cultural reasoning.

success_criteria: Student explains at least one reason why people in a given context make and experience drama
Student identifies that drama can communicate different things for different cultures or communities
